title: Checkpoint: Television
objective: After this level you can trace television from radio's networks to streaming and explain what drove each change.
summary: In 1961 FCC chairman Newton Minow called commercial TV a 'vast wasteland'. The chapter runs from radio's networks through filmed sitcoms, news, ratings, public TV, cable and streaming.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: one man called TV a 'vast wasteland'.
cards.body: In May 1961 the chairman of the FCC told the nation's broadcasters that commercial television was a 'vast wasteland'. Here is what he pushed for, and the whole chapter's story of television in one pass.

cards.headline: Minow's challenge
cards.body: Newton Minow, appointed FCC chairman by President Kennedy, told the National Association of Broadcasters in May 1961 that commercial television was a 'vast wasteland' and argued for public service TV. He encouraged the networks to expand their nightly news from 15 minutes to half an hour. He also pushed through the Educational Television Facilities Act of 1962, the first federal funds for educational TV, a step toward the Public Broadcasting Act five years later.

events.label: NBC's first radio network program reaches 21 cities
I Love Lucy debuts, shot on film in Hollywood
Ampex videotape begins to replace kinescopes
Johnson signs the Public Broadcasting Act
House of Cards releases a whole season at once

cards.headline: What drove each change
cards.body: CBS lured radio's stars to TV, and three networks made a unified mass culture. Filmed shows could earn money from reruns, and I Love Lucy's three cameras set the sitcom standard. Ratings set what each program's ads cost. Sesame Street aimed to get children ready for school. Then cable channels aimed at specialized interests split the audience, and streaming let viewers watch at their own pace.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: How American TV grew out of radio's networks, stars and sponsors.
Why filmed shows and videotape ended the era of live TV.
How ads and ratings paid for broadcast TV, and why public TV was created.
How cable and streaming split the network audience and changed how series are written.

questions.prompt: What did FCC chairman Newton Minow call commercial television in 1961?

options.label: Radio with pictures
options.rationale: That was an early description of TV, not Minow's phrase.

options.label: A 10-hour movie
options.rationale: That's how streaming writers describe a season.

questions.explanation: In May 1961 Minow told the National Association of Broadcasters that commercial TV was a 'vast wasteland'.

questions.prompt: From Level 73: what did Ampex introduce in 1956?

options.label: The first three-camera sitcom
options.rationale: That was I Love Lucy's method, from 1951.

options.label: The first practical videotape recorder for TV stations
The Audimeter for measuring viewers
options.rationale: Nielsen's Audimeter came from A.C. Nielsen.

questions.explanation: Ampex's 1956 videotape recorder replaced kinescope film.

questions.prompt: Why did shows recorded on film, like I Love Lucy, win out over live TV?

options.label: Live TV had been banned by the FCC
options.rationale: No ban appears in the chapter.

options.label: Film was cheaper than a live broadcast
options.rationale: The chapter gives reruns as the reason, not cost.

options.label: They could be shown again as reruns and keep earning money
Viewers couldn't tell live shows from filmed ones
options.rationale: The chapter doesn't make that claim.

questions.explanation: Filmed shows could earn income indefinitely from reruns; I Love Lucy became one of the first rerun series in 1955.

questions.prompt: From Level 76: besides setting ad prices, what do networks use ratings to decide?

options.label: Which actors win awards
options.rationale: Awards aren't decided by Nielsen ratings.

options.label: Which programs to keep or cancel
How long the evening news runs
options.rationale: The news grew to 30 minutes in 1963 for other reasons.

options.label: Which cities get cable
options.rationale: Ratings measure viewing, not cable service.

questions.explanation: Networks use ratings to set advertising rates and to decide which programs to continue or cancel.

questions.prompt: By 1956, movie attendance was down almost 50 percent from its 1946 peak (Level 49). By then, what share of US homes had a TV set?

options.label: About 20 percent
options.rationale: The chapter gives a much higher figure.

options.label: 100 percent
options.rationale: Not every home had a set.

questions.explanation: TV went from fewer than 2 percent of homes in 1948 to 70 percent by 1956, as movie attendance fell.
